study_a_sample_and_data: Jakarta, Indonesia (DKI Jakarta municipal utility PAM Jaya and 1998 private concessionaires Ondeo/Lyonnaise des Eaux and Thames Water). Mixed-methods dataset collected between 2001 and 2005 comprising: (1) a 2005 multi-stage stratified random household survey of N = 110 female respondents in poor households across 11 kelurahan (Kamal Muara, Penjaringan [Marlina & Gedong Kompa; Rawa Bebek], Pegangsaan Dua, Semanan, Kampung Melayu, Rawa Terate, Jati, Kampung Tengah, Kebon Melati, and Gunung Sahari Selatan) in six Jakarta neighborhoods; (2) >60 interviews in 2001, 2004, and 2005 with water managers, government officials, donors, and NGOs; (3) Dutch colonial archival research at KITLV (Leiden) and KIT (Amsterdam) in 2003; and (4) utility/regulatory reports (1998-2005) and GIS mapping of PAM Jaya tertiary network coverage against BPS census poverty data.
study_b_sample_and_data: Batavia/Jakarta, Indonesia (colonial artesian and spring-water municipal systems, postcolonial Ministry of Public Works and PAM Jaya, and post-1998 private concessionaires). Historical-institutional case study (pages 1-11 of 16 present before byte truncation) drawing on colonial and postcolonial archival records (1870s-1990s), PAM Jaya/JICA/JWSRB documents, 2005 North Jakarta fieldwork observations, and key-informant interviews from Kooy and Bakker's Jakarta water research programme; does not deploy the N = 110 household survey tables reported in Study A.
overlap_rationale: Both Study A (Bakker, Kooy, Shofiani, & Martijn, 2008, World Development) and Study B (Kooy & Bakker, 2008, Geoforum) draw from the same 2001-2005 Jakarta urban water research programme led by Bakker and Kooy and share substantial underlying archival, regulatory, and key-informant interview data, but differ in whether they include the 2005 quantitative household survey. Specifically, both papers analyze the exact same colonial archival records on Batavia (including the 1920 spring-water dual design standard of 140 L/day for 90% of European households vs 65 L/day for 33% of native residents, and the 1929 Eggink statistics of 6,926 kampung households receiving 24 L/s vs 10,392 European households receiving 84 L/s) and the same postcolonial historical and utility records on PAM Jaya and post-1998 private sector participation (including the 1950s-1960s Pejompongan I and II 3,000 L/s expansion along Jalan Thamrin-Sudirman, Hotel Indonesia, the Asian Games Complex, and Kebayoran Baru while excluding informal kampungs, and the 1965-1990 threefold treatment capacity increase delivering 40% of potential volume to under one-quarter of Jakarta's population). However, Study A additionally reports primary quantitative and qualitative results from a 2005 stratified random survey of N = 110 poor households across 11 kelurahan in six Jakarta neighborhoods (examining land tenure certificates, connection fees, transaction costs, and water expenditures) alongside PAM Jaya/BPS GIS network-density mapping, whereas Study B (pages 1-11 of 16 visible prior to byte truncation) relies on the archival and interview corpus to construct a detailed 1870-1998 historical genealogy of colonial and postcolonial governmentality. Because the archival and interview datasets overlap directly while the N = 110 household survey is unique to Study A, this pair represents partial sample/data overlap with moderate synthesis double-counting risk for city- and utility-level institutional/legal findings.

study_a_sample_and_data: Empirical input and calibration data from 5 urban water service delivery case studies conducted under Transparency International's TISDA program (GII 2011; TIK 2011; Bellaubi & Visscher 2014, 2016): 3 in Kenya—Old Town/Mombasa (MOWASCO), Migosi/Kisumu (KIWASCO) and Kangemi/Nairobi (NCWSC)—and 2 in Accra, Ghana—Madina and Nima (GWCL/AVRL). Participatory TAP (transparency, accountability, participation) scores, power/social-cost scores and WSDA user-end performance scores (totals 3, 4, 3, 2 and 3 out of 15) are used to parameterize and calibrate a deterministic 12-step monthly Agent-Based Model (NetLogo 4.1.3) simulating principal-agent game-theoretic social dilemmas across policy/regulation, provision and consumption levels.
study_b_sample_and_data: Qualitative institutional, power-asymmetry and governability ('water control') analysis of the exact same 5 urban water service delivery case studies from Transparency International's TISDA program (GII 2011; TI Kenya 2011; Bellaubi & Visscher 2014, 2016): 3 in Kenya—Old Town/Mombasa (MOWASCO), Migosi/Kisumu (KIWASCO) and Kangemi/Nairobi (NCWSC)—and 2 in Accra, Ghana—Madina and Nima (GWCL/AVRL). Data derive from formal interviews and informal discussions with public officials, utility managers and technicians, cross-checked with users, informal providers, community groups, donor/NGO staff and internal utility/regulatory documents, summarized via participatory TAP scores (0, 0.5, 1) and WSDA performance scores (totals 3, 4, 3, 2 and 3 out of 15).
overlap_rationale: Both full texts are complete and readable, and they are companion reports built on the exact same underlying five-site empirical dataset from Transparency International's Transparency and Integrity in Service Delivery in Africa (TISDA) program (citing GII 2011, TI Kenya 2011, and Bellaubi & Visscher 2014, 2016). Both papers examine the exact same three urban neighborhoods/utilities in Kenya—Old Town in Mombasa (MOWASCO), Migosi in Kisumu (KIWASCO) and Kangemi in Nairobi (NCWSC)—and the exact same two urban neighborhoods in Accra, Ghana—Madina and Nima (GWCL/AVRL). They reproduce the same empirical tables and findings: the main WSD actor-role matrix (Study A Table 4 vs Study B Table 5), the participatory Transparency, Accountability and Participation (TAP) scoring rubric and principal-agent relationship scores (Study A Table 1 and Figs. 1–2 vs Study B Tables 7–8), the Water Service Delivery Approach (WSDA) performance scores across the five sites (identical site totals of 3, 4, 3, 2 and 3 out of 15 in Study A Table 5 and Study B Table 6, with Continuity and Coverage row labels transposed in Study A), and the resulting corruption-risk and opportunistic/pragmatic management classifications across policy/regulation, provision and consumption levels (Study A Table 7 vs Study B Table 9). Study A explicitly cites Study B in manuscript form ('F. Bellaubi and F. Boehm 2016, unpublished manuscript', pp. 3, 12), while Study B (p. 20) points directly to agent-based modeling as the follow-on exploration. Analytically, Study B provides the qualitative institutional 'water control' and governability analysis of the five case studies, whereas Study A uses the same empirical TAP, power-asymmetry and WSDA performance scores to parameterize and calibrate a deterministic 12-month NetLogo 4.1.3 agent-based model; however, any synthesis extracting empirical WSD performance, TAP scores, corruption risks or management practices from both papers would double-count the identical five-case-study sample.

study_a_sample_and_data: Cross-sectional census of US community water systems serving >= 40,000 residents from US EPA SDWIS (N = 1,189 total: 1,055 local government and 134 investor-owned, serving 183,314,934 residents; analytical N = 1,183 in the 48 contiguous states). Single-family residential water rate schedules were collected independently in January–April 2019 and linked with 2017 ACS 5-year estimates (2013–2017) and 2009–2018 NOAA PDSI drought data. OLS regressions test the association of mean-to-median income inequality and private ownership with rate progressivity (Unit Price Ratio at 12,000–60,000 vs. 6,000 gallons/month).
study_b_sample_and_data: Cross-sectional census of the 500 largest US community water systems by service population from US EPA SDWIS across 48 states and DC (N = 500: 321 government-owned, 121 cooperative, and 58 investor-owned, serving ~140 million residents). Residential water rate schedules were compiled independently in January 2015 and linked with 2011–2015 ACS 5-year estimates (plus 2007–2011 ACS for population growth) and 2015 US Drought Monitor county data. OLS regressions test the association of private ownership, state PUC/pro-private regulation (NJ/PA), infrastructure age, and community socioeconomics (Gini, poverty) with typical annual household water bills (at 60,000 gallons/year) and lowest-quintile household income share spent on water.
overlap_rationale: Study A (Switzer & Teodoro 2025) and Study B (Zhang, González Rivas, Grant & Warner 2022) are independent studies by unrelated author teams that collected primary residential water rate schedules four years apart (January–April 2019 in Study A vs. January 2015 in Study B) and analyze distinct outcomes, but share a nested subset of approximately 500 large US community water systems. Specifically, both studies draw deterministic top-size censuses of US community water systems from the US EPA Safe Drinking Water Information System (SDWIS): Study A examines all 1,189 US utilities serving >= 40,000 residents (N = 1,183 in contiguous 48 states, serving 183.3 million people; ln(population) range 10.60 to 15.93), while Study B examines the 500 largest US community water systems across 48 states and DC (serving ~140 million people; ln(service population) range 11.36 [~85,800 residents] to 15.93). Consequently, nearly all 500 utilities in Study B are nested within Study A's 1,183-utility sample (~42% unit overlap and ~76% served-population overlap), sharing slow-moving SDWIS system attributes (private vs. public ownership, groundwater reliance) and partially overlapping 5-year ACS demographic windows (2013–2017 vs. 2011–2015). However, double-counting risk in synthesis is low because the tariff schedules were compiled independently in different cross-sectional years (2019 vs. 2015) and the dependent variables measure distinct constructs: Study A models rate-structure progressivity (the Unit Price Ratio of average unit price at 30,000 vs. 6,000 gallons/month), whereas Study B models annual water bill level ($ at 60,000 gallons/year) and lowest-quintile income share spent on water (%).

study_a_sample_and_data: Qualitative-historical genealogy of urban water supply in colonial Batavia and post-colonial/contemporary Jakarta, Indonesia (1870s–2006), based on 2003 colonial archival research in the Netherlands (Nationaal Archief in Den Haag, KITLV in Leiden, KIT in Amsterdam) and 2004–2006 Jakarta fieldwork comprising interviews with local and international water supply professionals, participant observation with NGOs in urban poor communities (kampungs), and discourse analysis of media, donor and utility documents (no numeric respondent N reported).
study_b_sample_and_data: Qualitative-historical case study of urban water supply fragmentation in colonial Batavia and post-colonial/contemporary Jakarta, Indonesia (1870–2007), drawing on the same Dutch colonial archival records (Amsterdam and Leiden), PAM Jaya/KIP/World Bank/JICA utility and policy reports, and Jakarta fieldwork interviews with water supply professionals and local/international NGO staff assisted by Endah Shofiani and E.J. Martijn (no numeric respondent N reported).
overlap_rationale: Both Study A (IJURR 2008) and Study B (Geoforum 2008, cited as forthcoming in Study A) are companion qualitative-historical case studies by Michelle Kooy and Karen Bakker derived from the exact same SSHRC-funded research project on colonial Batavia and post-colonial/contemporary Jakarta's water supply infrastructure. Both articles draw on the same 2003 Dutch colonial archival research in Amsterdam, Leiden and Den Haag and the same 2004–2006 Jakarta fieldwork (interviews with water supply professionals, participant observation with local and international NGOs, and policy/media document analysis) conducted with the same research assistants (Endah Shofiani and E.J. Martijn). While Study A frames the material around Foucauldian technologies of government, hygiene discourses and urban subjectivities and Study B critiques Graham and Marvin's 'splintering urbanism' thesis across four infrastructure periods, they analyze the same underlying archival corpus, fieldwork interviews, historical statistics (e.g., identical 1929/1930 Eggink kampung vs. European connection figures and contemporary 40,000 illegal connection estimates) and case setting.

study_a_sample_and_data: May–June 2013 fieldwork in Kisumu, Kenya comparing two DMM slums (Nyalenda A and Nyalenda B) with a non-DMM control slum (Manyatta B), using KIWASCO's list of individual water-kiosk providers as the sampling frame. Primary sample comprises N = 294 adult water-kiosk customers (109 Nyalenda A, 107 Nyalenda B, 78 Manyatta B; ANOVA df = 2, 291) interviewed at randomly sampled kiosks (text states 90 kiosks: 44 Nyalenda A, 28 Nyalenda B, 25 Manyatta B), supplemented by N = 46 water samples tested for total coliforms and E. coli (8 kiosks, 4 vendors, 12 wells/springs, 22 households) plus kiosk-level observations and operator interview responses on operating/disruption hours from the N = 103 kiosk sample (ANOVA df = 2, 100 in Section 3.1).
study_b_sample_and_data: May–June 2013 fieldwork in the same three Kisumu slums (Nyalenda A and Nyalenda B with DMM vs Manyatta B control), using KIWASCO's list of individual water-kiosk operators as the sampling frame. Primary sample comprises face-to-face interviews and kiosk observations with N = 103 randomly sampled water-kiosk operators (47 Nyalenda A, 26 Nyalenda B, 30 Manyatta B; ANOVA df = 2, 100) plus in-depth key informant interviews with N = 8 master operators (representing all 5 group and 3 individual master operators in Nyalenda A and B).
overlap_rationale: Both full texts are readable companion articles by Daniel M. Nzengya arising from the exact same May–June 2013 fieldwork project in three informal settlements in Kisumu, Kenya (Nyalenda A and Nyalenda B under KIWASCO's Delegated Management Model [DMM], compared against Manyatta B as a non-DMM control slum), conducted with the same three undergraduate research assistants and IRB approvals, and explicitly cross-referencing each other. The two papers primarily divide the study's respondent groups—Study B (2015) focuses on the supply side (interviews with N = 103 individual water-kiosk operators [47 Nyalenda A, 26 Nyalenda B, 30 Manyatta B; df = 2, 100] and N = 8 master-operator key informants), whereas Study A (2017/2018) focuses on the demand/user side (interviews with N = 294 adult water-kiosk customers sampled at those kiosks [109 Nyalenda A, 107 Nyalenda B, 78 Manyatta B; df = 2, 291] plus N = 46 microbiological water samples). However, the samples partially overlap rather than being completely disjoint: Study A Section 3.1 directly analyzes and reports kiosk-level observations and operator interview data from the N = 103 kiosk operator sample (queuing customers F(2, 100) = 3.63, containers F(2, 100) = 1.1, and operator-reported daily operating hours [11.6 h] and disruption hours [3.3 h]), and the 294 customers in Study A are nested within the same sampled KIWASCO kiosks evaluated in Study B on parallel outcomes (20-litre jerrican price and service disruption/reliability).

study_a_sample_and_data: San Sebastián de Yalí (SSY) municipality, Jinotega department, northern Nicaragua; fieldwork conducted over 41 days in 2012 across all 74 rural communities (22,500 residents), with empirical analysis focused on 5 illustrative communities (Communities A–E) containing 296 census households (Table 3: 154 served by CAPS and 142 self-provision; text p. 3 states 154 and 149) and N = 107 polled households (62 CAPS-served, 45 self-provision) via stratified random household surveys plus faecal coliform audits of water points/systems.
study_b_sample_and_data: Full text not accessible ([FULL TEXT NOT ACCESSIBLE — NO VERIFIED FULL-TEXT PDF COULD BE RETRIEVED]). Metadata and Study A's reference list identify it as Flores, Jiménez & Pérez-Foguet (2013), a local-level rural water access case study in Nicaragua published in International Journal of Water Resources Development 29(4):605-621, but its exact locality, data collection dates, sampling frame, and sample size (N) cannot be verified.
overlap_rationale: Study A (S285) has a readable full text reporting a 2012 fieldwork campaign in San Sebastián de Yalí municipality (Jinotega department, northern Nicaragua), where data were collected across all 74 rural communities over 41 days and analyzed in detail for a stratified subsample of 5 communities (N = 107 polled households out of 296 total households, split between CAPS-served and self-provision subgroups, combined with faecal coliform water-point/system audits). Study A cites Study B (Flores et al., 2013, International Journal of Water Resources Development 29(4):605-621) as prior work from which its human-right-to-water indicators were adapted and enhanced ("enhanced for this case study"). However, Study B (S310) has no accessible full text ([FULL TEXT NOT ACCESSIBLE — NO VERIFIED FULL-TEXT PDF COULD BE RETRIEVED]). Without Study B's full text, we cannot verify which Nicaraguan municipality or communities Study B examined, when its fieldwork occurred, its sample size (N), or whether any underlying household or water-point observations overlap with Study A's 2012 San Sebastián de Yalí dataset.

study_a_sample_and_data: Multi-level qualitative and administrative study of Tanzania's Rural Water Supply and Sanitation Program (RWSSP) combining Ministry of Water and PMO-RALG official interviews and national budget/coverage records (across 132 districts) with fieldwork conducted between July 2008 and August 2009 in 4 rural districts (Iramba, Nzega, Kigoma Rural and Same). Includes interviews with District Water Engineers and District Planning Officers, evaluation of 40 Phase 1 RWSSP village projects (10 per district), in-depth fieldwork in 4 wards across 2 districts (Mwakashanhala and Itobo in Nzega; Myamba and Hedaru in Same) involving ward/village/subvillage leaders, government officers, village plans and randomly selected villagers, plus brief interviews with ward officers in 50% of Same wards selected randomly.
study_b_sample_and_data: Full text not accessible. Citation metadata indicates a 2010 Natural Resources Forum article (34(2):93-105) by the same authors on Local Government Authorities and the human right to water in rural Tanzania, but the specific districts, fieldwork dates, sample size (N), respondent groups and empirical datasets cannot be verified.
overlap_rationale: Study A (S311) has a complete, readable full text examining resource allocation in Tanzania's Rural Water Supply and Sanitation Program (RWSSP) using national ministry interviews/documents, district budget allocation data, an analysis of 40 first-phase RWSSP projects (10 per district), and fieldwork conducted between July 2008 and August 2009 in four rural districts (Iramba, Nzega, Kigoma Rural and Same, with deeper ward/village fieldwork in Same and Nzega). Study A explicitly cites Study B as 'Jime´nez and Pe´rez-Foguet 2010b' on PDF pages 11 and 12 when discussing processes needed for village-level water information to influence Local Government Authority (LGA) priorities, indicating that both papers stem from the same authors' research programme on rural water governance in Tanzania. However, Study B (S315) has no accessible full text ('[FULL TEXT NOT ACCESSIBLE — NO VERIFIED FULL-TEXT PDF COULD BE RETRIEVED]'). Without Study B's full text, we cannot verify its exact districts, fieldwork dates, respondent groups, sample size, or empirical tables, and therefore cannot determine whether S311 and S315 analyze the exact same fieldwork sample, partially overlapping district/mapping data, or distinct samples.

study_a_sample_and_data: Systematic-style narrative literature review of N = 354 grey and academic documents published between 1985 and 2022 (searched across 4 academic and 35 grey databases using the SPIDER framework and coded in NVivo) examining household water poverty, affordability (3% and 5% disposable income thresholds), customer vulnerability, and utility bad debt in England and Wales. Secondary summary tables compile historical estimates from prior studies, including Bradshaw & Huby (2013).
study_b_sample_and_data: True full text not accessible due to a PDF retrieval mismatch: the file provided under Study B (SHA-256: 716a147031228c06b4ea094ff44085333f1df3889d94dbe4f4b47b61632ddcba) is another copy of Sylvester, Hutchings & Mdee (2023), DOI 10.2166/wp.2023.253, rather than Bradshaw & Huby (2013), DOI 10.1332/175982713X669835. Second-hand citations within Study A indicate Bradshaw & Huby (2013) analysed 2009/10 Department for Work and Pensions Family Resources Survey data for England and Wales, but Study B's primary sample size, methods, and results cannot be verified directly.
overlap_rationale: The PDF supplied for Study B (cited as Bradshaw & Huby 2013, Journal of Poverty and Social Justice 21(2):137-148, DOI 10.1332/175982713X669835) is a mismatched duplicate file identical byte-for-byte (SHA-256: 716a147031228c06b4ea094ff44085333f1df3889d94dbe4f4b47b61632ddcba) to Study A (Sylvester, Hutchings & Mdee 2023, Water Policy 25(5):492-511, DOI 10.2166/wp.2023.253). Because Study B's actual full text is missing/mismatched, mandatory audit rules require setting pair_classification to cannot_tell_missing_full_text, same_underlying_data to cannot_tell, and synthesis_double_counting_risk to cannot_tell. What can be verified from Study A's text alone is that Study A is a 2023 systematic-style literature review of 354 academic and grey documents (1985-2022) on water poverty in England and Wales that explicitly cites and summarises Bradshaw & Huby (2013) (reporting 2009/10 Family Resources Survey water poverty prevalence of 23.6% at the 3% threshold and 11.5% at the 5% threshold, and mean water poverty gaps of £3.46 and £3.62). However, without the authentic full text of Bradshaw & Huby (2013), Study B's exact sample size, analytical specifications, and primary empirical tables cannot be directly verified, and the retrieval error in the corpus would cause Study A's text to be read twice if uncorrected.

study_a_sample_and_data: Primary household survey of N = 3,714 households across four Indian cities—Ahmedabad (Gujarat, n = 1,000), Bengaluru (Karnataka, n = 1,000), Hyderabad (Telangana, n = 1,000) and Kochi (Kerala, n = 714)—funded by a UGC-UKIERI grant (conceived 2012–2013, workshops in 2016), supplemented by secondary data from Census of India (2001, 2011), Central Water Commission (2015), ADB (2007) and city water utilities (PDF Pages 1–68 of 318 accessible; Pages 69–318 truncated).
study_b_sample_and_data: Not accessible in prompt: '== STUDY B FULL TEXT ==' (Roy, Akshintala & Sharma, 2013, Social Change) was completely cut off by prompt truncation ('<truncated 53508 bytes>' at PDF Page 68 of Study A), so geography, dates, sample size (N), unit of analysis and dataset cannot be verified.
overlap_rationale: Study A (Rout & Kattumuri, 2022; S600) is a 318-page Springer monograph whose text in the prompt is readable from PDF Page 1 through PDF Page 68, where the prompt ends with '<truncated 53508 bytes>'. Because of this truncation inside Study A, '== STUDY B FULL TEXT ==' (Roy, Akshintala & Sharma, 2013; S799) was completely omitted from the prompt and is not accessible. What CAN be verified from Study A's accessible chapters (Preface, Contents, Lists of Figures/Tables, Chapter 1 including Section 1.6 'A Note on Methodology', and Chapter 2) is that Study A analyzes a primary household survey of N = 3,714 urban households across four Indian cities—Ahmedabad (n = 1,000), Bengaluru (n = 1,000), Hyderabad (n = 1,000) and Kochi (n = 714)—funded by a UGC-UKIERI partnership grant (conceived during 2012–2013 at LSE with workshops in June–August 2016), alongside secondary data from the Census of India (2001, 2011), Central Water Commission (2015), ADB (2007) and municipal water utilities (AMC, BWSSB, HMWSSB, KWA). Metadata also show non-overlapping author teams and publication dates nine years apart (Rout & Kattumuri 2022 vs Roy, Akshintala & Sharma 2013). What CANNOT be verified without Study B's full text (and PDF Pages 69–318 of Study A) is whether Study B reports primary fieldwork or secondary urban water statistics (e.g., Census/NSSO/ADB city-level indicators), which Indian cities or utilities Study B examines, its sample size and dates, and whether any empirical tables or secondary series overlap. Per strict audit rules prohibiting guessing from titles/metadata alone when either full text is inaccessible, pair_classification is set to 'cannot_tell_missing_full_text'.

study_a_sample_and_data: Systematic scoping review of N = 88 publications (84 peer-reviewed, 4 grey literature; published 1946–2017 across 44 countries and the Occupied Palestinian Territories) addressing environmental health conditions, exposures, outcomes, obstacles, and recommendations in the transitional phase of forcible displacement (6 months to 2 years), drawn from a master pool of 307 eligible publications identified from searches on 12 October 2017 (peer-reviewed) and 6 January 2018 (grey literature). Only 28 of the 88 included publications focused exclusively on the transitional phase.
study_b_sample_and_data: Systematic scoping review of N = 213 publications (198 peer-reviewed, 15 grey literature; published 1946–2017 across 54 countries) addressing environmental health conditions, exposures, outcomes, obstacles, and recommendations in protracted forcible displacement (>2 years), drawn from the exact same master pool of 307 eligible publications (10,324 peer-reviewed records searched 23 September–12 October 2017 and 100 grey literature records searched 23 December 2017–6 January 2018; 6,949 screened; 1,125 full-text assessed).
overlap_rationale: Both Study A (Cooper et al., 2021) and Study B (Behnke et al., 2020) are companion systematic scoping reviews produced by the same UNC Water Institute team from the exact same master literature search and screening pipeline (10,324 peer-reviewed records searched up to 12 October 2017 + 100 grey literature records searched up to 6 January 2018; 6,949 unique records screened; 1,125 full texts assessed; 307 total eligible publications). From that shared 307-publication pool, the team partitioned publications into emergency (n = 104), transitional (n = 88, analyzed in Study A), and protracted (n = 213, analyzed in Study B) displacement phases, explicitly noting in Study B Table 3 that the phase counts sum to 405 rather than 307 because multi-phase publications were included in more than one review, and noting in Study A that only 28 of its 88 publications (32%) focused exclusively on the transitional phase. Consequently, up to 60 publications overlap across phases, and multiple specific primary studies—including those cited for legal/policy and institutional obstacles (e.g., Mohamed et al., 2014; UNICEF and Hydroconseil, 2017; Schuller and Levey, 2014; Tota-Maharaj, 2016; Toole and Waldman, 1990; Milton et al., 2017; Cronin et al., 2008, 2009)—are extracted and synthesized in both reviews.

study_a_sample_and_data: Sector-wide policy and institutional review of urban water supply and sanitation in Sri Lanka (urban population 3.8 million in 1998, with emphasis on Greater Colombo, Kandy, Galle, Jaffna, and Puttalam), drawing on 1985–1998 government and donor reports (NWSDB, Presidential Task Force 1995, OECF/JICA 1997, ADB 1998) covering 275 water supply schemes across 24 districts in 1997, projected Colombo water demand (1995–2020), capital investment scenarios, and NWSDB rising-block tariffs.
study_b_sample_and_data: National regulatory and sector performance review of urban water and sanitation services in Chile (16,812,391 urban residents served by 28 main private and concessionary water companies, plus 278 wastewater treatment systems), synthesizing administrative and benchmarking data from the national regulator Superintendencia de Servicios Sanitarios (SISS) spanning 1998–2015 (principally 2007–2015 quality indicators, tariffs, Casen-targeted household subsidies, and non-revenue water).
overlap_rationale: Both full texts are complete and match their respective citations. Study A (Seneviratne 2000) examines urban water supply, sanitation, tariff cross-subsidization, and public utility performance in Sri Lanka (focusing on Greater Colombo, Kandy, Galle, Jaffna, Puttalam, and 275 water supply schemes across 24 Sri Lankan districts using 1985–1998 sector reports). Study B (Molinos-Senante 2018) is a book chapter analyzing legal reforms, utility privatization, hypothetical efficient-company tariff regulation, and service quality benchmarking across 28 urban water and sanitation companies in Chile regulated by the Superintendencia de Servicios Sanitarios (SISS) using 1998–2015 administrative data. The two studies have different authors, continents, decades, institutional settings, and underlying data sources (likely flagged as a candidate pair only because both titles feature 'Urban Water Management' and both start on page 131).

study_a_sample_and_data: Qualitative key-informant interview study (N = 30 interviews conducted by Davison Muchadenyika in June–July 2013 across Harare, Bulawayo, Masvingo, Mutare and Marondera: 5 central government ministry officials, 6 local authority officials, 5 urban social movement actors, 3 political party representatives, 6 NGO/international agency staff and 5 planners/consultants/researchers), combined with secondary analysis of legislation, parliamentary reports and Auditor-General/fiscal data (2005–2016) on ZINWA water/sanitation centralisation and ZINARA vehicle licensing centralisation in urban Zimbabwe.
study_b_sample_and_data: Post-2017 ('Second Republic', circa 2019) mixed-methods primary survey and qualitative study across four purposively selected urban local authorities representing all four tiers of Zimbabwean urban councils (Bulawayo City Council, Chitungwiza Municipality, Zvishavane Town Council and Epworth Local Board). Primary data comprise N = 100 usable closed-ended questionnaires (out of 120 distributed to Ministry of Local Government officials, municipal employees and randomly selected service consumers), open-ended questionnaires, focus group discussions (5–10 participants per group, including UCAZ and Residents' Associations) and in-depth interviews with senior council managers.
overlap_rationale: Study A (Muchadenyika & Williams, 2018) and Study B (Marumahoko et al., 2020) are unrelated, empirically distinct studies conducted by completely separate research teams at different institutions, in different time periods, and using different designs and samples. Study A is a qualitative and institutional analysis based on 30 key-informant interviews conducted by Davison Muchadenyika in June–July 2013 ( primarily in Harare, Bulawayo, Masvingo, Mutare and Marondera) supplemented by secondary fiscal and Auditor-General records up to 2016, focusing on the centralisation of water/sanitation (ZINWA) and vehicle licensing (ZINARA). Study B is a post-Mugabe ('Second Republic', circa 2019) mixed-methods survey and fieldwork study across four purposively sampled urban local authorities (Bulawayo City Council, Chitungwiza Municipality, Zvishavane Town Council and Epworth Local Board), analyzing 100 usable closed-ended questionnaires (from 120 distributed), open-ended questionnaires, focus group discussions and in-depth interviews with municipal employees, officials and service consumers. Although both examine urban local governance and service delivery in Zimbabwe, they share no underlying primary empirical dataset or fieldwork sample.

study_a_sample_and_data: Cluster-randomized controlled trial (AEARCTR-0004648; PACTR202102616421588) of the 'Healthy Villages' component of DRC's Healthy Villages and Schools (VEA) programme in four provinces (Kongo Central, Kasai, Kasai Central, South Kivu): 332 rural villages grouped into 121 clusters (50 intervention clusters with 146 villages; 71 control clusters with 186 villages), randomized March–June 2018. Long-term (median 3.6-year post-intervention) follow-up survey conducted November 2022–April 2023 (field interviews Nov 24, 2022–Feb 10, 2023) across 329 villages and N = 3,283 households (head woman interviewed), comprising 1,133 re-interviewed respondents from the 2019 5-month follow-up (plus 140 replacement households and 39 new respondents in Wave 1 households) and 1,970 newly sampled households (6 per village), with child diarrhea assessed for N = 4,072 children under 5 (in 2,466 households), length-for-age Z-score measured for N = 2,142 children (in 2,374 eligible households), WASH institutions index measured in N = 329 villages, plus water-point and household E. coli/coliform testing and structured handwashing observations.
study_b_sample_and_data: Cluster-randomized controlled trial (AEARCTR-0004648) of the 'Healthy Villages' component of DRC's Healthy Villages and Schools (VEA) programme in the same four provinces (Kongo Central, Kasai, Kasai Central, South Kivu): 332 rural villages grouped into 121 clusters (50 treatment clusters, 71 control clusters). Short-term (median 5-month / 151-day post-intervention) follow-up survey conducted October 11–December 23, 2019 across N = 328 villages (145 treatment, 183 control) and N = 1,312 households (4 per village; 580 intervention, 732 control; head woman interviewed), alongside a concurrent village chief and WASH committee leadership survey (N = 328 villages) and child health module (N = 1,388 children aged 10–59 months).
overlap_rationale: Study A (Quattrochi et al., 2025, PLOS Medicine) and Study B (Quattrochi et al., 2021, BMJ Global Health) are companion follow-up reports of the exact same cluster-randomized controlled trial (AEARCTR-0004648) evaluating the DRC's national Healthy Villages and Schools (Villages et Ecoles Assainis, VEA) programme across the exact same 121 clusters (50 treatment clusters, 71 control clusters; 332 randomized rural villages) in four provinces (Kongo Central, Kasai, Kasai Central, and South Kivu). Study B reports the short-term (median 5-month post-intervention) survey wave conducted in October–December 2019 among 1,312 households (4 per village) and village/WASH leaders across 328 villages. Study A explicitly cites Study B as the first-round 5-month follow-up (Ref. 26) and reports the long-term (median 3.6-year post-intervention) survey wave conducted between November 2022 and February/April 2023 across 329 of the same trial villages, interviewing 3,283 households—comprising 1,133 re-interviewed respondents (86% of Study B's 1,312 households, plus replacement/new-respondent Wave 1 households) alongside 1,970 newly sampled households (6 per village). Because both studies estimate intention-to-treat effects of the identical randomized intervention on the identical 121 village clusters (with 86% household panel retention plus augmented household sampling at Wave 2) across overlapping outcomes (improved water source, improved sanitation facility, WASH/water governance index, water satisfaction, handwashing/hygiene behavior, cost of water, school attendance, and child diarrhea/health), treating them as independent studies in evidence synthesis creates a high risk of double-counting the same trial.

study_a_sample_and_data: Qualitative interpretive phenomenological study in George Compound (peri-urban Lusaka, Zambia) using criterion-based purposive sampling and reflexive thematic analysis of 50-60 minute in-depth and key informant interviews with N = 29 participants: 25 community beneficiaries (10 males, 15 women, coded GC) who experienced government/Lusaka Sanitation Program interventions over the past 10 years and 4 key informants (coded KII) across the Ward Development Committee, Water and Sanitation Committee, Lusaka City Council (Public Health Department), ZEMA (Inspectorate), NWASCO, and LWSC (Peri-Urban Department).
study_b_sample_and_data: Qualitative phenomenological study in George Compound (peri-urban Lusaka, Zambia) using the exact same criterion-based purposive sample and reflexive thematic analysis of 50-60 minute in-depth and key informant interviews with N = 29 participants (10 males, 15 women beneficiaries coded GC, and 4 key informants from WDC, Water and Sanitation Committee, LCC, ZEMA, NWASCO, and LWSC), reporting the gendered exclusion and mitigation subset of findings.
overlap_rationale: Both papers are readable full texts published in the same November 2025 issue of International Journal of Research and Innovation in Social Science (Vol. 9, Issue 11; both received 14 November 2025 and accepted 22 November 2025) by the exact same author team (Mwale, Kanyamuna, Moose, and Simui) from James Mwale's PhD thesis at the University of Zambia. They are companion reports ('salami-sliced' articles) analyzing the exact same qualitative fieldwork sample in George Compound, Lusaka, Zambia: N = 29 total participants (10 male and 15 female sanitation programme beneficiaries plus 4 key informants from LCC, ZEMA, NWASCO, LWSC, WDC, and the Water and Sanitation Committee). Both papers share word-for-word identical Background, Methodology, Study Limitations, Suggestions for Future Studies, and Reference sections. Empirically, Study A reports the broader set of institutional, regulatory, infrastructural, and gendered mitigation themes (including KII quotes from ZEMA, LCC, NWASCO, and LWSC alongside beneficiary quotes), whereas Study B extracts and reframes the gendered exclusion/mitigation subset from the exact same interviews—reproducing verbatim the same participant quotes (e.g., GC 6, GC 11, GC 19, and GC 22) and entire Discussion subsections from Study A, while adding one quote on absentee landlords (GC 11). Treating them as independent studies in qualitative or quantitative synthesis would directly double-count the same respondents and verbatim interview excerpts.

study_a_sample_and_data: Qualitative case study in two peri-urban localities of the Greater Accra Metropolitan Area (GAMA), Ghana—Oduman (Ga West Municipality) and Pantang (La Nkwantanang-Madina Municipality)—conducted between August and November 2015 under the BMBF WaterPower project. Data include 62 semi-structured household interviews across original villages (n = 13) and new settlement sites (n = 49) encompassing 25 local private water providers, plus interviews with traditional authorities (3), elders (9), youth organisation members (3), and landowner associations (2), supplemented by transect walks, 1-week photo diaries in 4 households, and background expert interviews on land/water institutional setup.
study_b_sample_and_data: Practice-based ethnographic and qualitative governance study of mobile tanker water supply across urban and peri-urban Accra (GAMA), Ghana, conducted between August and November 2015 and August to September 2017 under the BMBF WaterPower project. Data include 12 days of ride-along participant observation, mapping, semi-structured interviews, and informal conversations by the first author (R. Alba) with tanker truck drivers, truck owners, and mates across four organized tanker associations (three urban in North-West and East Accra/Adenta, one peri-urban) plus individual drivers, together with 15 in-depth interviews with municipal officials, GWCL engineers and field staff, PURC members, MWRWH Water Directorate officials, and World Bank staff.
overlap_rationale: Both papers have complete, readable full texts and originate from the same research group (Governance and Sustainability Lab, Trier University) under the BMBF-funded WaterPower project (grant 01 LN 1316 A) in the Greater Accra Metropolitan Area (GAMA), with Study B citing Study A as reference [13]. Despite sharing the broader research programme and an initial August–November 2015 fieldwork window, their primary empirical samples, geographies, respondent groups, and analytical designs are distinct. Study A examines household-level land and domestic water access and customary land/local water control in two specific peri-urban localities (Oduman and Pantang; August–November 2015), drawing on 62 household interviews (which included 25 local/neighbourhood water providers), 17 interviews with traditional authorities, elders, youth-group members, and landowner associations, 4 household photo diaries, transect walks, and background institutional expert interviews. Study B (led by R. Alba, who conducted the field investigation across August–November 2015 and August–September 2017) examines urban water governance and mobile tanker brokerage across urban and peri-urban Accra, drawing on 12 days of ride-along participant observation and interviews with tanker truck drivers, mates, and truck owners across four tanker associations (primarily urban North-West and East Accra/Adenta plus one peri-urban association) alongside 15 in-depth interviews with municipal, GWCL, PURC, MWRWH Water Directorate, and World Bank officials. At most, some background water-sector expert interviews in late 2015 may have been conducted jointly by the project team (used only as institutional context in Study A, where only a Stool Lands official is cited, versus formal governance analysis in Study B), so double-counting risk in synthesis is low.

study_a_sample_and_data: Logit and Box-Cox instrumental-variable cost analysis of municipal waterworks adoption across N = 244 cities (50 building, 194 not building; cost IV estimated on n = 106) in four northwestern Prussian provinces (Rhineland, Westphalia, Hannover, and Holstein) during 1880-1887, combining Grahn (1898) waterworks data, 1883/84 Prussian municipal class/income tax data (Herrfurth & von Tzschappe 1884), 1882 county steel employment, and 1866-1867 cholera mortality records, alongside cross-national descriptive comparisons of typhoid mortality (1877-1910) and municipal sanitary infrastructure expenses ca. 1906-1912 in German and U.S. cities.
study_b_sample_and_data: Published 3-page summary of Brown's 1987 PhD dissertation covering urban housing and sanitation reform in Germany (1870-1910) across two empirical datasets: (1) hedonic rent, market-segmentation (Chow test), and household housing/sanitation demand models estimated on a sample of N = 600 apartments from the 1889 cantonal housing census of Basel, Switzerland; and (2) a simultaneous-equation median-voter model of municipal waterworks diffusion across Prussian cities from the post-1867 cholera era onward using Prussian tax-weighted electoral representation, capacity costs, median voter income, and industrial water demand.
overlap_rationale: Both full texts are readable and authored by John C. Brown as part of the same research programme originating in his 1987 University of Michigan PhD dissertation (explicitly cited in Study A, footnote 23). Study B is the published 3-page Journal of Economic History dissertation summary covering Germany (and Basel) from 1870 to 1910, comprising two distinct empirical components: (1) a hedonic rent and housing demand analysis of N = 600 apartments from the 1889 housing census in Basel, Switzerland (absent from Study A), and (2) a simultaneous-equation median-voter analysis of municipal waterworks diffusion in Prussian cities under the Three-Class franchise system from the post-1867 cholera period onward. Study A (Urban Studies, 1989) expands and adapts that Prussian waterworks diffusion dataset and political-representation framework to compare Three-Class provinces (Rhineland, Westphalia) against restricted-equal-franchise provinces (Hannover, Holstein) across N = 244 northwestern Prussian cities (50 building, 194 not building) during 1880-1887, supplemented by cross-national comparisons of typhoid mortality (1877-1910) and municipal water/sewer burdens ca. 1906-1912 in Germany, Great Britain, France, and the United States. Thus, the Prussian (especially Rhenish) municipal waterworks diffusion data and Three-Class electoral analysis partially overlap, while each study also contains substantial non-overlapping data and scope.

study_a_sample_and_data: Ethnographic fieldwork across 32 rural Indian villages in four states: 12 villages in 2 districts of Madhya Pradesh (including Shivpuri), 15 villages in 3 districts of West Bengal, 3 villages in 1 district of Bihar, and 2 villages in 1 district of Jharkhand (SIDA-funded project). Sample comprises 162 women and 149 men (N = 311 informants) via participant observation, key-informant interviews, 12 focus group discussions (5 women-only), 4 village case studies, 55 handpumps in 17 villages (MP, Bihar, Jharkhand), 15 women trained as handpump mechanics under TRYSEM, and 12 village Panchayats in MP.
study_b_sample_and_data: Ethnographic fieldwork conducted between 2002 and 2004 across 27 rural Indian villages in two states: 12 villages in 2 districts of Madhya Pradesh (Datia and Shivpuri; examining PRI Women and Child Welfare and Health Committees and 12 village Panchayats, including villages Lamkana and Saprar) and 15 villages in 3 districts of West Bengal (examining NGO-initiated community arsenic removal plant committees, including village Raipara), using participant observation, interviews, and 12 focus group discussions (5 women-only).
overlap_rationale: Both papers are readable full-text articles published by Nandita Singh in Volume 10 of Gender, Technology and Development (2006) drawing on the same SIDA-funded rural Indian water ethnographic research programme, with Study B's entire 27-village sample nested inside Study A's 32-village sample. Specifically, Study B analyzes 12 villages in two districts of Madhya Pradesh (Datia and Shivpuri) and 15 villages in three districts of West Bengal (2002-2004 fieldwork), including 12 focus group discussions (five women-only). Study A analyzes those exact same 12 villages in two districts of Madhya Pradesh and 15 villages in three districts of West Bengal—plus 3 villages in one district of Bihar and 2 villages in one district of Jharkhand (32 villages total; 162 women and 149 men; the exact same 12 FGDs including five women-only). Furthermore, both papers report identical empirical findings from the overlapping Madhya Pradesh/West Bengal fieldwork, including the exact 30% female attendance rate across 12 village Panchayats, two village PRI handpump siting cases where SC women were excluded by upper-caste siting (named Lamkana and Saprar in Study B), and women's nominal membership in NGO-led arsenic removal plant committees in West Bengal, while Study A additionally reports handpump rejection and 15 TRYSEM-trained women mechanics across MP, Bihar, and Jharkhand.

study_a_sample_and_data: Historical archival case study of the collectivized Barcelona Water Company (Sociedad General de Aguas de Barcelona, SGAB) in Barcelona, Spain during the Spanish Civil War (1936–1939). Primary data comprise SGAB archival correspondence from 1936–1940 (12 boxes, ~8,000 documents), SGAB annual reports (1936–1939), Barcelona City Council and Generalitat official proceedings/decrees (1930–1938), 1930s press clippings (La Vanguardia, Solidaridad Obrera, Luz y Fuerza), and N = 2 interviews with retired SGAB workers conducted in 2009 and 2011.
study_b_sample_and_data: Contemporary institutional and fiscal case study of the regional water cycle in Metropolitan Barcelona and the Inland Basins of Catalonia, Spain (focusing on 1999–2012, with wastewater plant series 1973–2009 and budget/debt/tariff series 2000–2012). Units of analysis are regional public water agencies—Agència Catalana de l'Aigua (ACA) and bulk supplier Aigües Ter-Llobregat (ATLL)—analyzed via ACA annual budgets and reports (2000–2011), ATLL policy reports, Catalan government budgets and decrees, statistical databases, and 2011–2012 newspaper and trade-union/official statements.
overlap_rationale: Both full texts are accessible and share two co-authors (Hug March and David Saurí), a broader geographical setting (Barcelona/Catalonia, Spain), and funding from the same Spanish CICYT grant (CSO2009-12772-C03-01 / CSO2009-12772-03-01). However, they investigate completely distinct historical eras, institutional actors, and empirical datasets with zero sample overlap. Study A (Gorostiza, March & Saurí 2013) is a historical archival study of the retail utility Sociedad General de Aguas de Barcelona (SGAB) under worker collectivization during the Spanish Civil War (1936–1939), drawing on 1936–1940 company correspondence (12 archival boxes, ~8,000 documents), 1930s press clippings, municipal proceedings, and two interviews with retired SGAB workers. Study B (March & Saurí 2013) is a contemporary political-economic and fiscal study of regional water governance in Metropolitan Barcelona and Catalonia (primarily 2000–2012), analyzing how EU environmental directives and regional water-tax financing drove public debt at the Catalan Water Agency (ACA) and bulk supplier Aigües Ter-Llobregat (ATLL), leading to the 2011–2012 private leasing tender of ATLL, using 2000–2011 Catalan/ACA budgets, ATLL policy reports, statistical series, and 2011–2012 press reports.

study_a_sample_and_data: Not verifiable — full text not accessible. Metadata indicates a 2026 study by Koros, Juuti, Juuti and Mutie on safe water and sanitation access in urban periphery and low-income areas in Kenya.
study_b_sample_and_data: Not verifiable — full text not accessible. Metadata indicates a 2026 study by Koros, Juuti, Juuti and Asokan on small-scale water services in Kenya.
overlap_rationale: Neither Study A (S008) nor Study B (S009) has an accessible full text or abstract in the prompt (both are marked '[FULL TEXT NOT ACCESSIBLE — NO VERIFIED FULL-TEXT PDF COULD BE RETRIEVED]'). From metadata alone, it can be verified that both papers share three authors (Koros JK, Juuti PS and Juuti RP), appear in Public Works Management & Policy in 2026 under distinct DOIs (10.1177/1087724X251356460 and 10.1177/1087724X261447370) with different fourth co-authors (Mutie J vs Asokan SM), and both address water services in Kenya. Without readable full texts, however, exact study sites, data collection dates, sampling frames, sample sizes (N), respondent groups, and analytical datasets cannot be verified, making it impossible to determine whether the two studies share underlying empirical data.

study_a_sample_and_data: Agincourt HDSS, Bushbuckridge Local Municipality, Mpumalanga, South Africa (VAPAR programme). Three-stage qualitative PAR design: Stage 1 (June–September 2017, 8 community workshops with 16 community co-researchers in the water-nominating village / 48 community participants + 4 researchers = 52 across 3 villages, combined with 2014/15 Agincourt VA mortality data); Stage 2 (January–March 2018, 3 multisectoral analysis workshops in Mbombela/Agincourt with n=18, 17, and 18 community, MDoH, other provincial/district government, and researcher participants); and Stage 3 (September–October 2018, 2 local action-planning workshops at Agincourt HDSS offices with n=19 and 20 community, government, water agency, NGO, and researcher stakeholders).
study_b_sample_and_data: Agincourt HDSS, Bushbuckridge Local Municipality, Mpumalanga, South Africa (VAPAR programme). Stage 1 community PAR and Photovoice study (8 weekly consensus-building workshops; dates reported in Study A as June–September 2017) across 3 villages (24 initial + 24 newly recruited = 48 community participants aged >=18), focusing on the 1 village ('Village A') that nominated lack of clean, safe water (n=8 original community stakeholders + n=8 newly recruited women of reproductive age = 16 community co-researchers).
overlap_rationale: Both full texts report sequential, nested stages of the same Verbal Autopsy with Participatory Action Research (VAPAR) cycle on lack of safe water in the Agincourt Health and Socio-Demographic Surveillance System (HDSS), Bushbuckridge Local Municipality, Mpumalanga, South Africa. Study B (Hove et al., 2019) reports Stage 1 alone: 8 weekly community PAR and Photovoice workshops (June–September 2017) with 16 community stakeholders in the village that nominated clean water (8 initial participants plus 8 newly recruited women of reproductive age, within a 3-village cohort of 48 community participants). Study A (Hove et al., 2021) reports the full multi-stage process: it explicitly incorporates Stage 1 (tabulating the 8 community workshops with N=52 including 4 researchers in Table 1, citing Study B as reference [37] as the prior publication of Stage 1 results, and summarizing those Stage 1 community findings alongside 2014/15 Agincourt VA mortality data in its Results), and then extends the empirical data to 3 multisectoral analysis workshops in January–March 2018 (n=18, 17, 18) and 2 district-level action-planning workshops in September–October 2018 (n=19, 20) involving provincial/district government departments, NGOs, researchers, and a subset of the Stage 1 community stakeholders. Because Study B's sample and qualitative outputs form Stage 1 of Study A while Study A adds five 2018 multisectoral workshops with additional government/NGO actors, there is partial sample and data overlap.

study_a_sample_and_data: Narrative synthesis and secondary-data policy review of urban water resilience in the Hindu Kush Himalaya (HKH) conducted under the HI-AWARE (CARIAA) consortium. No primary survey or fieldwork sample (N) is reported. Compiles secondary municipal water supply and demand data (in MLD) and major water issues in Table 1 for N = 8 cities across 6 countries: Kabul (Afghanistan), Quetta (Pakistan), Shimla, Mussoorie, and Nainital (India), Kathmandu (Nepal), Xining (China), and Thimphu (Bhutan), alongside narrative discussion of Pokhara, Baglung, Almora, Leh, Srinagar, Manali, Gangtok, Dharamshala, Dehradun, Haldwani, and Phuentsholing using published literature, government reports (e.g., NITI Aayog 2018), and media sources up to 2019.
study_b_sample_and_data: Literature and national-census review of urbanisation definitions, migration/tourism drivers, water supply deficits, and household/government coping and adaptation strategies across the HKH regions of 4 countries (Bangladesh, India, Nepal, and Pakistan), conducted under the HI-AWARE (CARIAA) consortium. No primary survey sample (N) is collected. Analyzes secondary national census datasets—Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (2011), Census of India (2001, 2011), Nepal Central Bureau of Statistics (2001, 2011), and Pakistan Bureau of Statistics (1981, 1998)—and compiles secondary municipal water demand, supply, and deficit data (in MLD) in Table 9 for N = 13 urban centres: Rangamati (Bangladesh); Baramula, Shimla, Mussoorie, Darjeeling, and Kohima (India); Tansen, Kathmandu Valley (KUKL), and Pokhara (Nepal); and Quetta, Rawalpindi, Mansehra, and Karak (Pakistan).
overlap_rationale: Both full texts are accessible and represent two distinct review/synthesis articles produced under the same Himalayan Adaptation, Water and Resilience (HI-AWARE / CARIAA) research consortium and published in the same special issue of Water Policy, 22(S1) (2020), by completely different author teams (Vishal Singh and Anvita Pandey at CEDAR in Study A vs. Sreoshi Singh, S. M. Tanvir Hassan, Masooma Hassan, and Neha Bharti at ICIMOD/BCAS/PARC/TERI in Study B). Study A explicitly cites the online-first version of Study B (Singh et al., 2019). Neither paper reports a primary household or official survey sample; instead, both synthesize secondary municipal water statistics and published/grey literature across Hindu Kush Himalaya (HKH) cities. However, they exhibit partial overlap in their compiled city-level water demand-and-supply datasets and case-study narratives: 4 of the 8 cities tabulated in Study A Table 1 (Quetta, Shimla, Mussoorie, and Kathmandu) are also among the 13 cities tabulated in Study B Table 9, with identical or rounded-identical secondary MLD figures for Quetta (170 MLD demand, 106 MLD supply) and Mussoorie (14.4 vs. 14.5 MLD demand; 7.67 vs. 7.7 MLD supply), as well as the exact same 210 MLD shortage figure for Kathmandu Valley in the text (plus shared qualitative discussion of Pokhara, Almora, Leh, and Srinagar). At the same time, each paper covers substantial non-overlapping material: Study A extends to Afghanistan (Kabul), China (Xining), Bhutan (Thimphu, Phuentsholing), and Nainital and formulates 12 urban water governance/resilience recommendations (including groundwater bye-law enforcement against informal tanker markets), whereas Study B conducts a census-based demographic and urban-definition analysis (1981-2011) across Bangladesh, India, Nepal, and Pakistan and includes 9 cities not in Study A's table (Rangamati, Baramula, Darjeeling, Kohima, Tansen, Pokhara, Rawalpindi, Mansehra, and Karak). Consequently, there is partial underlying secondary-data overlap and a moderate risk of double-counting city-level MLD deficits and case observations for the shared HKH towns.

study_a_sample_and_data: Quantitative in-person household contingent valuation (CV) survey conducted in June–August 2012 (following focus groups and a 30-household pilot) with a random sample of N = 500 households in the town of San Lorenzo, San Marcos, Guatemala (37.2% served by the municipal water system and 62.8% served by 10 rural community-based water organizations [CBWOs]; econometric estimation samples of N = 177 municipal households and N = 260 communal households using bivariate probit and univariate probit models of willingness to pay and willingness to work).
study_b_sample_and_data: Qualitative semi-structured one-to-one interviews conducted in June–July 2008 with a purposeful sample of N = 12 Guatemalan government officers directly involved in drinking water provision (9 municipal-level officers across multiple municipalities and 3 national-level policy officers), complemented by content analysis of official and technical water-sector documents.
overlap_rationale: Both papers are authored by William F. Vásquez (Fairfield University) on drinking water governance and service quality in Guatemala, and Study A cites Study B (Vasquez, 2011) for institutional context, but the two studies use completely distinct empirical samples, respondent populations, fieldwork periods, and research designs. Study A analyzes quantitative contingent valuation survey data collected in June–August 2012 from a random sample of 500 households in San Lorenzo, San Marcos (177 municipal-system households and 260 community-managed water system households in the econometric models). Study B analyzes qualitative semi-structured interviews conducted in June–July 2008 with a purposeful sample of 12 government officials (9 municipal water officers across high- and low-altitude cities and 3 national-level water policy officers), supplemented by official document analysis. There is no shared underlying sample or double-counting risk.

study_a_sample_and_data: 22 months of ethnographic fieldwork (2007–2010) in northern Mumbai settlements in Jogeshwari (Premnagar, Meghwadi, and Banjrekar Wadi) and BMC water supply department headquarters and ward offices; qualitative interviews and participant observation with settlers (e.g., Rane), party workers/councilors (e.g., Surve), hydraulic/maintenance engineers (e.g., Patkar, Kerkar), plus the resident documentary film Pyasa Premnagar (Shaikh 2008). No fixed quantitative N reported.
study_b_sample_and_data: 22 months of ethnographic fieldwork (2007–2010) in northern Mumbai settlements in Jogeshwari (focusing on Premnagar in comparison with Meghwadi and Banjrekar Wadi) and BMC water department ward offices; qualitative interviews and participant observation with Premnagar residents (e.g., Asif, Salim), licensed/informal plumbers (e.g., Rafiq-bhai, Abdul, Ahmed), and municipal water engineers (e.g., Rane, Gupte), plus the resident documentary film Pyasa Premnagar (Shaikh 2008). No fixed quantitative N reported.
overlap_rationale: Both Study A (Anand 2011) and Study B (Anand 2012) are companion ethnographic articles written by Nikhil Anand drawing on the exact same 22-month ethnographic fieldwork conducted in Mumbai between 2007 and 2010, supported by the identical four funders (Stanford University, Social Science Research Council, Wenner-Gren Foundation, and National Science Foundation). Both papers investigate the same Jogeshwari settlements in northern Mumbai—specifically Premnagar, Meghwadi, and Banjrekar Wadi—alongside the same Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai (BMC) water supply department and ward offices. While Study A frames the broader technopolitics of 'hydraulic citizenship' and water pressure across Marathi-Hindu settlements and Muslim-majority Premnagar (highlighting the January 1995 cutoff rule, application documentation, councilor patronage, illegal connections, booster pumps, and revitalized wells), Study B explicitly cites Anand (2011) three times and zooms in on Premnagar's 'municipal disconnect' and abjection through the interactions of residents, plumbers, and BMC engineers. Both articles analyze the same legal/administrative barriers, infrastructure failures, informal/illegal tapping, booster pump usage, and return to subterranean bore wells, including shared testimony from the 2008 resident documentary 'Pyasa Premnagar' (Shaikh 2008) and near-verbatim passages describing Premnagar's return to neighborhood wells. Treating them as independent empirical studies in synthesis would double-count the same fieldwork site and sample.

study_a_sample_and_data: Ethnographic fieldwork from a nine-month study of two informal settlements in Mumbai (four months per site), focusing empirically on one site—Rafinagar (northeastern Mumbai, adjacent to Shivaji Nagar in M-East ward)—covering the November/December 2009 water raids and January–March 2010 interviews with residents (e.g., Salma/Resident A, Residents B and C, Govind), NGO director Leena Joshi, and clinic doctor Ravindra Rathod, combined with secondary media and policy analysis across Mumbai (including Dahisar/New Link Road). Funded by ESRC (RES-0360-7277).
study_b_sample_and_data: Nine-month comparative ethnographic fieldwork in two informal settlements in Mumbai: non-notified Rafinagar in the northeast (~4,000 households, 6 toilet blocks/76 seats; Part 1 and Part 2, noting developments up to 2011) and notified Khotwadi in the northwest (~2,000 households, 24 toilet blocks/180 seats). Data comprise participant observation and repeated interviews with residents (e.g., Salimbhai, Naina, Mumtaz in Rafinagar; Shobha, Lakshmi, Prabha, and garment workers in Khotwadi), municipal staff, NGOs, and CBOs regarding sanitation and water entitlements. Funded by ESRC (RES-062-23-1669).
overlap_rationale: Both papers are readable full texts by overlapping author teams (Graham, Desai, and McFarlane 2013; McFarlane and Desai 2015) drawing on the same nine-month ethnographic fieldwork conducted across two contrasting informal settlements in Mumbai (four months per site, plus observation and unstructured/repeated interviews with residents, NGOs, and officials). However, their analytical samples only partially overlap. Study A empirically reports ethnographic fieldwork from only one of the two fieldwork settlements—Rafinagar (a non-notified, predominantly Muslim settlement in northeast Mumbai), specifically examining the late 2009 to March 2010 BMC/police water raids, water rackets, and post-raid water scarcity—alongside citywide media and policy discourse analysis covering Shivaji Nagar, Dahisar/Ganpat Patil Nagar, and Mumbai's bottled-water/leisure sectors. Study B analyzes the full two-settlement comparative fieldwork sample—both Rafinagar (approx. 4,000 households) and Khotwadi (an authorized, predominantly Marathi settlement of approx. 2,000 households in northwest Mumbai)—focusing primarily on moral economies and 'sites of entitlement' around public, private, and CBO-managed toilet blocks, drain cleaning, and water access. Study B explicitly cites Study A (note 22) when recounting the 2009 BMC/police water raids and temporary BMC water tanks in Rafinagar, and also notes a 2011 MHADA toilet block in Rafinagar Part 2 and a different ESRC grant code (RES-062-23-1669 vs RES-0360-7277 in Study A). Because the Rafinagar ethnographic fieldwork (including the pre-1995 slum cut-off rule, 2009 water raids, and temporary tank installation) is shared across both papers while Khotwadi (~half of Study B) and citywide media cases (in Study A) are unshared, this is a classic multi-site partial sample overlap with moderate double-counting risk for Rafinagar water findings.

study_a_sample_and_data: Full text not accessible ([FULL TEXT NOT ACCESSIBLE — NO VERIFIED FULL-TEXT PDF COULD BE RETRIEVED]). From metadata alone, S309 is a 2023 International Journal of the Commons article on informal water distribution, collective agency and self-organization in informal areas of Xochimilco, Mexico City; specific settlements, fieldwork dates, sample size (N) and empirical methods cannot be verified.
study_b_sample_and_data: Two informal settlements in the southern Conservation Zone of Xochimilco municipality, Mexico City (Amplicación Tizilclipa and San José Obrero). Data collected in 2017 (semi-structured interviews with government officials) and 2018–2019 (community leaders and residents), comprising N = 27 key-informant semi-structured interviews (17 community/parada leaders, 5 local Alcaldía government officials/piperos, and 3 Mexico City government officials from SACMEX, CORENA and SEDEMA) plus N = 41 resident questionnaires (20 in San José Obrero and 21 in Amplicación Tizilclipa), coded in MAXQDA 2018.
overlap_rationale: Study A (S309: Hernandez, Manuel-Navarrete, Lerner & Siqueiros 2023, International Journal of the Commons) has no accessible full text in the audit packet ([FULL TEXT NOT ACCESSIBLE — NO VERIFIED FULL-TEXT PDF COULD BE RETRIEVED]). Study B (S676: Hernández Aguilar, Lerner, Manuel-Navarrete & Siqueiros-García 2021, Water International) has a complete, readable 20-page full text examining water supply narratives in two informal settlements in Xochimilco, Mexico City (Amplicación Tizilclipa and San José Obrero) based on 27 semi-structured key-informant interviews (2017–2019) and 41 resident questionnaires (2018–2019). Although the citation metadata of Study A shares the same core research team (Hernández, Manuel-Navarrete, Lerner and Siqueiros) and general geographic setting (informal areas of Xochimilco, Mexico City), it cannot be verified without Study A's full text whether S309 analyses the exact same 2017–2019 fieldwork sample in Amplicación Tizilclipa and San José Obrero, a partially overlapping sample, or distinct data collection. Per strict audit rules, pair_classification, same_underlying_data, and synthesis_double_counting_risk are set to cannot_tell.

study_a_sample_and_data: Qualitative case study of water governance, institutional reforms and public utility performance (SEDAPAL and regulator SUNASS) in Lima, Peru (1990s–2000s). Primary data come from a research fieldtrip conducted between March and June 2009 comprising archival and policy document review (SEDAPAL, SUNASS, National Library), visits to peripheral barriada communities (e.g. Pachacútec in the North Cone), observation of public events and interviews with local residents, regulators, policy-makers and multilateral agency representatives (exact interview sample size N not reported), combined with secondary utility/official statistics (SEDAPAL 2005, 2008; INEI; ICOM 2001).
study_b_sample_and_data: Full text not accessible ([FULL TEXT NOT ACCESSIBLE — NO VERIFIED FULL-TEXT PDF COULD BE RETRIEVED]). Citation metadata identifies a 2012 Geoforum article by A.A.R. Ioris on urban development and water problems in Lima, Peru, but fieldwork dates, sampling frame, sample size (N) and empirical data sources cannot be verified.
overlap_rationale: Study A (Ioris 2012, Singapore Journal of Tropical Geography) is readable in full text (author's peer-reviewed manuscript) and reports a qualitative institutional case study of water governance and neoliberal reforms in Lima, Peru, drawing on a March–June 2009 research fieldtrip (policy/archival review at SEDAPAL, SUNASS and the National Library, visits to peripheral communities including Pachacútec, attendance at public events and interviews with local residents, regulators, policy-makers and multilateral agency representatives). Study B (Ioris 2012, Geoforum) is marked [FULL TEXT NOT ACCESSIBLE — NO VERIFIED FULL-TEXT PDF COULD BE RETRIEVED]. While the shared author, publication year and Lima water-sector focus suggest potential overlap with the March–June 2009 fieldwork, it is impossible to verify from full texts whether Study B uses the exact same interview/fieldwork sample, a partial subset or distinct data.

study_a_sample_and_data: Qualitative ethnographic and theory-building multiple case study of three neighbourhoods and their community-based organizations (CBOs) in the metropolitan area of Cochabamba, Bolivia: Site A in Sacaba (297 households; service cooperative, initially a water committee), Site B in Quillacollo (215 households; OTB, initially a water committee), and Site C in Cercado (339 households; junta vecinal). Primary data were collected during 5 months in 2013 and 2 months in 2014 via observations, spontaneous ethnographic interviews, and 69 formally arranged audio-recorded interviews with 47 distinct informants (CBO leaders, members, and 3 cooperative employees at Site A), supplemented in early 2018 by 9 semi-structured follow-up interviews (3 per site).
study_b_sample_and_data: Full text not accessible ([FULL TEXT NOT ACCESSIBLE — NO VERIFIED FULL-TEXT PDF COULD BE RETRIEVED]). Metadata identifies Study B as Ida Helgegren's 2020 PhD thesis at Chalmers University of Technology on water supply and sanitation systems in the Kanata Metropolitan Region (Cochabamba), Bolivia, but specific samples, datasets, fieldwork dates, and whether it is a monograph or article-compilation thesis cannot be verified without the full text.
overlap_rationale: Study A (S410) has a complete, readable 24-page full text (Helgegren et al., 2020, International Journal of Water Resources Development), whereas Study B (S420, Helgegren 2020 PhD thesis at Chalmers University of Technology) is marked [FULL TEXT NOT ACCESSIBLE — NO VERIFIED FULL-TEXT PDF COULD BE RETRIEVED]. Can be verified from Study A's full text and metadata: both works share the same first/sole author (Ida Helgegren at Chalmers University of Technology), publication year (2020), and general topical/geographic area (water and sanitation systems in metropolitan Cochabamba / Kanata Metropolitan Region, Bolivia; Swedish compilation PhD theses at Chalmers commonly incorporate journal articles such as S410 alongside additional studies). Cannot be verified without Study B's full text: whether Study B is a compilation thesis that reprints or synthesizes Study A verbatim, whether Study B includes additional empirical fieldwork or distinct stakeholder samples beyond the three CBO case studies in Study A, or the exact sample overlap and double-counting risk. Following strict isolation and missing-full-text audit rules, pair_classification, same_underlying_data, and synthesis_double_counting_risk are set to cannot_tell.

study_a_sample_and_data: Lilongwe, Malawi (Lilongwe Water Board [LWB] in-house connection regime and LWB-Water Users Association [WUA] kiosk regime). Qualitative multi-phase fieldwork conducted in 2008-2009, 2013-2014 (Nov 2013-Jan 2014), and 2017-2018 (Oct 2017-June 2018), comprising semi-structured interviews with representatives of the Government of Malawi (GoM), LWB (including Kiosk Management Unit), seven WUAs, local NGOs, and residents of two low-income areas (LIAs), supplemented by 2018 documentary screenings and 2006-2018 tariff, revenue, and WUA financial surplus records (exact total interview N not reported).
study_b_sample_and_data: Lilongwe, Malawi (Lilongwe Water Board [LWB] centralized piped water network across northern, central, and southern zones). Qualitative fieldwork conducted over four months in 2014 comprising N = 38 semi-structured interviews with LWB employees from operators and engineers to managers (plus a Ministry representative and international expert), participatory hotspot mapping of service continuity, a focus group discussion, and participant observation following LWB technical staff in daily operation and maintenance activities.
overlap_rationale: Both studies are readable full texts produced under the same two research programmes—UNHIDE and Horizon 2020 Marie Sklodowska-Curie INHAbIT Cities (Grant No. 656738)—by overlapping author teams (Cecilia Alda-Vidal and Maria Rusca) studying the same municipal utility, the Lilongwe Water Board (LWB) in Lilongwe, Malawi (and citing the same city-level baseline figures: 78% network coverage split between 44% in-house connections and 56% water kiosks). However, their empirical fieldwork datasets, respondent samples, legal/operational exposures, and outcomes are distinct. Study A (Pihljak et al., 2019/2021) examines the multi-level governance and negotiation of water tariffs across three fieldwork waves (2008-2009 on WUA establishment; Nov 2013-Jan 2014 comparative tariff interviews corresponding to Pihljak's 2014 MSc thesis; and Oct 2017-June 2018 follow-up interviews and 2018 documentary screenings conducted after Study B's February 2017 online publication), interviewing GoM officials, LWB/Kiosk Management Unit staff, seven WUAs, NGOs, and residents of two LIAs alongside 2006-2018 tariff and WUA financial records. Study B (Alda-Vidal et al., 2017/2018) is an ethnographic and participatory mapping study conducted over four months in 2014 comprising 38 semi-structured interviews with LWB technical operators, engineers, and managers, a focus group discussion, and participant observation of physical operation and maintenance (backup line diversions, pressurized take-offs, unrecorded valve operations, and repair prioritization) shaping spatial inequalities in supply continuity and pressure. Study A also cites Study B (Alda-Vidal et al., 2018) and Pihljak's 2014 thesis is cited separately in Study B. Double-counting risk is low because the designs, respondent groups, and outcomes (water pricing vs physical O&M continuity) are distinct, though systematic reviewers aggregating at the city or utility level should note both examine the same single utility (LWB).

study_a_sample_and_data: Ethnographic and documentary study in Mumbai, India, focusing on K-East ward (Andheri East, population ~806,360) and the Mumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC) Hydraulic Engineering Department. Draws on nearly two years of ethnographic fieldwork (specific vignettes dated June–December 2007 and February 2008) plus audit documents from the 2004–2007 World Bank-funded Water Distribution Improvement Project (WDIP) conducted by Castalia Strategic Advisors. No fixed quantitative N; qualitative sample comprises World Bank management consultants (e.g., Haresh), senior BMC water engineers, and field shadowing of ward water engineer Patankar and maintenance crews/councilors.
study_b_sample_and_data: Ethnographic study in Premnagar ('Squatters Colony'), a predominantly Muslim settlement (>40,000 registered adult voters) in Jogeshwari, northern Mumbai, India, and the local BMC ward water office. Based on 22 months of fieldwork conducted between 2007 and 2010 (specific vignettes dated late 2007 to December 2008). No fixed quantitative N; qualitative sample comprises Muslim settlers/households in Premnagar (e.g., Asif, Salim, Abdul, women's savings group), local plumbers mediating legal and unauthorized connections (e.g., Rafiq-bhai, Ahmed), and BMC ward/city water engineers (e.g., Rané, Gupte, Assistant Engineer).
overlap_rationale: Both articles are single-authored ethnographies by Nikhil Anand (supported by the same SSRC, Wenner-Gren, and NSF grants) drawing on the same overarching ~2-year ("nearly two years" / "22 months") ethnographic fieldwork conducted in Mumbai between 2007 and 2010 on the Mumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC) water supply system in northern Mumbai. Part of the underlying fieldwork sample and institutional data is shared: both papers draw on interviews and ethnographic observations with BMC ward and city water engineers during 2007–2008 and report shared institutional findings regarding Mumbai's pre-1995 residency cutoff rule for slum water eligibility, non-functioning water meters (over half not working, leading to estimated bills), and municipal engineers' discretionary handling of unauthorized connections and leaks. However, each article analyzes a substantially distinct actor subset, focal site, and empirical case within that multi-site fieldwork without any overlapping named/pseudonymous informants or vignettes: Study A examines the 2004–2007 World Bank/Castalia Water Distribution Improvement Project (WDIP) water audit controversy in K-East ward through consultant interviews (Haresh), senior BMC planning engineers, and field visits with ward engineer Patankar, whereas Study B examines municipal disconnection and infrastructural abjection in the Muslim settlement of Premnagar (Jogeshwari) through interviews and observations with Muslim settlers (Asif, Salim, Abdul), plumbers (Rafiq-bhai, Ahmed), and BMC engineers (Rané, Gupte). Because both draw on the same 2007–2010 BMC fieldwork in northern Mumbai with overlapping municipal-utility/engineer ethnography alongside distinct community vs consultancy sub-samples, this pair represents partial sample overlap with moderate synthesis double-counting risk if city/utility-level findings on legal cutoffs, metering, and informal connections are pooled as independent studies.

study_a_sample_and_data: Mabalane district, Gaza Province, Mozambique (Limpopo Basin), evaluating the PRONASAR pilot programme (2011-2013; fieldwork/fee records from 2012-2013 under the CPWF Limpopo Basin Development Challenge). Three-step mixed-methods dataset: (1) programme document review and interviews with national, provincial and district actors; (2) qualitative village-level survey in 12 communities across three water-access zones (village leader interviews, water committee focus groups, transect walks to water structures, and women's focus groups in 2 villages); and (3) stratified random household survey of N = 119 respondents (20% per wealth quartile across 4 leader-ranked wealth groups) in 3 riverine villages (36, 66 and 16 interviews; plus 2012 fee ledger records for 275 registered households in Village 1 and an 18-option card preference exercise).
study_b_sample_and_data: Mabalane district, Gaza Province, Mozambique (Limpopo Basin), evaluating the PRONASAR pilot programme (fieldwork in second half of 2012 and post-2013 flood follow-up, triangulated with 2012 UEM water-point mapping across 64 district villages). Same three-step mixed-methods dataset: (1) institutional/document analysis and interviews with national, provincial, district and NGO actors; (2) qualitative village-level survey in the same 12 communities (18.4% of district villages) across the seven localities and three water-access zones (leader interviews, water-point manager/committee focus groups, infrastructure walks, and women's focus groups in 2 villages); and (3) the same stratified household survey of n = 119 families (20% sampled from 4 leader-defined wealth groups) in 3 riverine communities, including the 18-option preference exercise and water-fee/source questions.
