overlap_rationale: Both Study A (Ducrot 2017, Physics and Chemistry of the Earth) and Study B (Ducrot & Bourblanc 2017, Natural Resources Forum) are distinct companion journal articles analyzing the exact same three-stage empirical study of the pilot PRONASAR rural water supply programme (2011-2013) in Mabalane district, Gaza Province, semi-arid Mozambique. Both papers rely on: (1) institutional document review and key informant interviews with national, provincial, district and NGO actors conducted in 2012-2013; (2) qualitative fieldwork in the exact same 12 villages across Mabalane's three water-access zones (leader interviews, water committee focus groups, infrastructure walks and women's focus groups in two villages); and (3) the exact same wealth-stratified household survey (N = 119 interviews, sampling 20% of households across four leader-classified wealth groups) in three riverine villages, including the same 18-option card preference exercise (e.g. 39% rejecting small reservoir rehabilitation in both papers, matching village household count discrepancies such as the 69-household village, and matching water-fee timeliness and saline borehole vs river reliance by wealth group). Whereas Study A focuses on village-level water committee functioning, leadership and institutional bricolage, Study B analyzes distributive, procedural and contextual equity across district planning, contractor drilling allocation and community maintenance.

study_a_sample_and_data: Qualitative legal-political case study and secondary-data synthesis (no primary survey N) focused on Johannesburg and Phiri, Soweto (2001-2009), examining Suez's 2001-2006 Johannesburg Water management contract, Free Basic Water block tariffs (6 kl/month in 2001; 10 kl/month indigent policy in 2008), prepayment water meters, and the Mazibuko v City of Johannesburg litigation (2008 High Court, 2009 SCA, October 2009 Constitutional Court), supplemented by secondary figures on Durban tariff elasticity (1997-2004, Bailey & Buckley 2005), national water disconnections (1.5 million/year by 2003, Muller 2004), SAPS service delivery protests (2009-2012, >800/year), HSRC polls (2003-2011), and global Climate Justice conferences (2000-2012).
study_b_sample_and_data: Macro-historical qualitative political-economy synthesis and secondary-data review (no primary survey N) of urban township social movements in South Africa from the mid-1980s to 2011 (centring on Soweto, Alexandra, Vaal, East Rand, Orange Farm, and Durban), covering 1984-1994 civic associations and rent/bond boycotts (~80 regional civics in 1990), post-1994 demobilisation, 2001-2003 Soweto Electricity Crisis Committee campaigns against Eskom disconnections (20,000 households/month; R1.4bn arrears cancelled in 2003), 2001-2003 Johannesburg/Orange Farm water tariff and prepaid meter conflicts, secondary statistics from Statistics SA (1995-2002), SALDRU (1993-2008), Bond & Dugard 2008 on Durban water consumption (1998-2004) and 1.5 million/year water disconnections, and Police Gatherings Act protest counts (>8,000/year since 2005).
overlap_rationale: Both Study A (Bond 2013, SAJHR) and Study B (Bond 2012, Third World Quarterly) are single-authored qualitative political-economy and legal-policy case-study essays by Patrick Bond rather than primary microdata surveys, and they have distinct overarching scopes: Study A critiques human-rights versus 'commons' advocacy narratives through the 2001-2009 Johannesburg/Soweto (Phiri) water commercialisation and Mazibuko v City of Johannesburg litigation alongside 2000-2012 global Climate Justice summits, whereas Study B traces urban township 'people power' across South Africa from the mid-1980s anti-apartheid civic movement (rent and bond boycotts, ACO, CAST, SANCO) to late-1990s/2000s struggles over Soweto electricity (SECC/Eskom disconnections and R1.4 billion arrears write-off), Orange Farm water meters, HIV treatment, and 2005-2011 Gatherings Act protests. However, for post-2000 municipal service delivery, both papers examine the same Johannesburg Free Basic Water tariff case (the 2001 6,000 litres/month free block with a steeply convex second block, Suez, APF, and 20,000 households/month disconnections) and cite the same underlying secondary empirical statistics (1.5 million people disconnected from water annually and the 1997/98-2004 Durban real water price doubling reducing consumption among the poorest third of residents), creating partial overlap in case-study and secondary empirical evidence.

study_a_sample_and_data: Case study of water sector commercialization/corporatization (1997-2001) in the Cape Town and Tygerberg administrations, Cape Metropolitan Area, South Africa, based on 9 months of PhD dissertation fieldwork in 2000-2001 comprising interviews with ~100 local authority officials, politicians, union shop stewards, and civil society representatives; N = 120 stratified household interviews across four Coloured and African townships (including Langa, Khayelitsha, and Mitchells Plain); municipal water tariff schedules (1997-2002); and municipal billing/disconnection data (N = 159,886 household water cutoffs in 1999-2001: 16,964 in Cape Town and 142,922 in Tygerberg).
study_b_sample_and_data: Case study of water commercialization and cost recovery (1997-2001) in the Cape Town and Tygerberg administrations, Cape Metropolitan Area, South Africa, based on 2000-2001 fieldwork by the first author: N = 120 semi-structured household interviews conducted in 2001 across four Coloured and African townships (Langa and Mitchells Plain in Cape Town; Khayelitsha and Bonteheuwell in Tygerberg; 30 per township across standpipe, yard tap, and in-house neighbourhoods, including N = 90 billed and N = 57 in-arrears subsamples), a 2000 metro-wide water depot audit, official interviews/communications, and municipal water disconnection/reconnection data (N = 159,886 water cutoffs in 1999-2001: 16,964 in Cape Town and 142,922 in Tygerberg).
overlap_rationale: Both papers are companion articles reporting empirical findings from the exact same 2000-2001 PhD dissertation fieldwork by Laila Smith (at Clark University, where Study B co-author Susan Hanson was based) examining commercialization/corporatization and cost-recovery water policies over 1997-2001 in the Cape Town and Tygerberg administrations of the Cape Metropolitan Area, South Africa. Both studies draw on the same stratified household interview sample of N = 120 households across the same four Coloured and African townships (Langa, Mitchells Plain, Khayelitsha, and Bonteheuwell, stratified by standpipes, yard taps, and in-house connections), the same municipal official interviews/fieldwork, and the exact same 1999-2001 municipal water disconnection records (159,886 total cutoffs: 16,964 in Cape Town and 142,922 in Tygerberg, including 77,000 in 2001, 14,355 in Khayelitsha over six months, 902 per 1,000 billed customers in Mumfuleni, and a 60% illegal reconnection rate in Tygerberg). Study A explicitly cites Study B (Smith and Hanson, 2003) and directly reprints Figures 5 and 6 of Study B as Figures 4 and 5 of Study A, while framing three cost-recovery policies (pricing/tariffs, outsourcing, and debt management/cutoffs) alongside ~100 institutional interviews; Study B provides fuller tabular and regression/discriminant analyses of the N = 120 household survey focusing on infrastructure underinvestment and debt management/cutoffs.

study_a_sample_and_data: Qualitative ethnographic case study of a local bazaar association (Bazaar Management Committee / bazaar somiti) in an inner-city bosti on 0.23 km2 of government land in Dhaka (>15,000 families, ~400 bazaar shops), conducted over 7 months between 2008 and 2010 via overnight stays in a rented house, observation, a Venn-diagram exercise, 20 key informant interviews, interviews with 8 committee/somiti leaders, the water-vending family, 20 water users (10 room owners and 10 tenants), 2 ward commissioners, the ruling-party ward president, DWASA and DESCO field staff, 5 CBO members and 3 NGO field staff.
study_b_sample_and_data: Qualitative grounded-theory ethnographic study of the same inner-city bosti on government land in Dhaka (pseudonym 'Boshoti', ~100,000 inhabitants), conducted over ~9 months across four years (2008-2011, with brief February and April 2012 eviction observations) while living in a rented room in the settlement, using theoretical sampling, observation of salish disputes and unstructured interviews with inhabitants, local water vendors (~50 operating in Boshoti), CBO/BOSC members, local association and political party leaders, 2 ward commissioners, NGO field staff (including DSK) and DWASA officials.
overlap_rationale: Both papers are readable full texts by Shahadat Hossain originating from the same DFG-funded doctoral research project ('The Struggle for Urban Livelihoods and the Quest for a Functional City') at TU Dortmund and studying the exact same large inner-city bosti on government land in Dhaka (unnamed in Study A, >15,000 families; pseudonymized as 'Boshoti' in Study B, ~100,000 inhabitants; Study B explicitly cross-references Study A in endnote 25). Both papers rely on ethnographic residence in a rented room in the settlement and overlapping interviews with bazaar association leaders, water vendors, room owners, tenants, CBO members, NGO field staff, two elected ward commissioners and DWASA staff, and both recount the 2003 shop-owner overthrow of local mastaan (musclemen) in the bazaar, the creation of the bazaar committee, its acquisition of the settlement's sole officially approved DWASA water connection used to shield illegal lines and water price markups of 10 to 15 times the official DWASA rate. However, the underlying sample overlap is partial (nested longitudinal expansion) rather than identical: Study A reports interim fieldwork covering seven months between 2008 and 2010 focused specifically on the bazaar association (committee/somiti) and its regulation of bazaar water and DESCO electricity supply, whereas Study B reports completed doctoral fieldwork covering roughly nine months across four years (2008 to 2011, plus 2012 eviction observations) and expands beyond the bazaar committee to examine settlement-wide informal land allocation/transactions, roughly 50 water vendors across Boshoti and NGO/donor water initiatives (BOSC/UNICEF tube wells and the 2009-2010 DSK-DWASA-ADB network extension), without examining electricity supply.

study_a_sample_and_data: Qualitative and small-N mixed-methods case study of WaterAid-initiated Water Users Associations (WUAs) in peri-urban Lilongwe, Malawi (including Chinsapo, Mtandire/Mtsiliza, Kauma, Area 50, Mgona, Chimutu III, Tsabango, Area 24, Area 41). Fieldwork conducted November 2008–February 2009 and November 2013–January 2014: N = 48 semi-structured interviews (WaterAid London and Malawi staff, Lilongwe Water Board/KMU officials, WUA representatives, key informants), focus group discussions (WUAs, CBOs, NGO partners), and N = 30 semi-structured household consumer questionnaires.
study_b_sample_and_data: Interdisciplinary mixed-methods political ecology and water-quality study of Lilongwe Water Board's centralized water network in Lilongwe, Malawi (UNHIDE and Horizon 2020 INHAbIT Cities projects). Fieldwork conducted September/November 2014–February 2015 and February–April 2016: N = 80 interviews (urban planners, LWB managers/staff, MBS, kiosk attendants, residents), UNHIDE-INHAbIT household survey of n = 497 in six administrative areas (March–April 2016), and laboratory microbiological/physicochemical analysis (E. coli, total coliforms, turbidity, free/total chlorine) of N = 170 water samples from two low-income areas (Area 56, Area 7) and two higher-income areas (Area 47, Area 2).
overlap_rationale: Both full texts are accessible and authored by Maria Rusca (with different co-author teams) studying urban water supply in Lilongwe, Malawi (Lilongwe Water Board network and kiosks), but they draw on completely non-overlapping fieldwork periods, distinct datasets, and different analytical designs. Study A (Rusca et al. 2015) examines institutional bricolage and elite capture in WaterAid-supported Water Users Associations (WUAs) using fieldwork conducted from November 2008 to February 2009 and November 2013 to January 2014 (48 semi-structured interviews, focus group discussions, and 30 household questionnaires). Study B (Rusca et al. 2017) examines physicochemical and microbiological drinking water quality inequalities across Lilongwe's centralized water network using later fieldwork conducted between September/November 2014 and February 2015 and February to April 2016 under the UNHIDE and Horizon 2020 INHAbIT Cities projects (80 interviews, the March-April 2016 UNHIDE-INHAbIT survey of n = 497 households across six administrative areas, and 170 laboratory water samples from Areas 2, 7, 47 and 56). Because data collection waves, samples, and outcomes are empirically distinct, there is no shared sample or double-counting risk.

study_a_sample_and_data: Qualitative semi-structured face-to-face interviews and direct observations conducted in summer 2015 with N = 60 piped-water households (44 male household heads, 16 female spouses; residency 3-28 years, mean 9 years) across 12 residential districts in Phases I (38%), II (33%) and III (28%) of Abuja City, Nigeria, recruited from 18 key informants (>=10 years residency) via snowball sampling.
study_b_sample_and_data: Qualitative semi-structured interviews and field observations conducted between 2013 and 2015 in Abuja City, Nigeria, with N = 115 interviewees comprising 85 piped-water residents (53 male, 32 female; residency 3-28 years, mean ~10 years) across 14 residential districts in Phases I (n = 25), II (n = 32) and III (n = 28)—recruited from 18 participating key informants (>=10 years residency) via snowball sampling—plus 30 city officials from the Abuja Water Board (18) and FCTA engineering department (12).
overlap_rationale: Both papers are readable qualitative fieldwork studies of domestic piped water services in Abuja, Nigeria, conducted by Ismaila Rimi Abubakar, and exhibit clear partial sample overlap. Study B (2016) analyzes interviews conducted between 2013 and 2015 with 85 adult piped-water residents across 14 residential districts (25 Phase I, 32 Phase II, 28 Phase III; 53 male, 32 female) plus 30 city water/engineering officials. Study A (2018) analyzes interviews conducted in summer 2015 with 60 household heads or spouses across 12 residential districts (~23 Phase I, ~20 Phase II, ~17 Phase III; 44 male, 16 female) and no officials. Critically, both papers describe the exact same initial seed of 18 key informants with at least 10 years of residency in Abuja, the exact same three snowball-sampling eligibility criteria (adult/household head or spouse, piped water connection at home, and >=3 years at current residence), the exact same respondent residency span (3 to 28 years), and an overlapping 2015 fieldwork window, with every geographic and gender subgroup count in Study A fitting as a subset within Study B's 85-resident sample while excluding Study B's 25 additional residents and 30 city officials. Although Study A cites Study B as an earlier study and focuses on household coping strategies and regulatory/socioeconomic determinants rather than Study B's seven utility service-quality and governance dimensions, both draw on overlapping Abuja household interview data and report overlapping observations on spatial inequity across city phases, flat-rate billing, water quality/treatment, and vending/fetching.

study_a_sample_and_data: Ethnographic fieldwork in 32 rural Indian villages across four states: 12 villages in two districts of Madhya Pradesh, 15 villages in three districts of West Bengal, 3 villages in one district of Bihar and 2 villages in one district of Jharkhand (with long-term residential fieldwork in 3 core villages). Sample comprises 162 women and 149 men (total N = 311 informants) interviewed or participating in 12 focus group discussions (5 women-only) and 4 village case studies; specific sub-analyses cover 55 handpumps across 17 villages in MP, Bihar and Jharkhand (24 rejected), 46 handpumps in MP and Bihar (9 in backward-section localities), arsenic/fluoride removal plants in WB and MP, 15 women trained as handpump mechanics and 12 village panchayats (PRIs). Fieldwork dates are not explicitly stated (SIDA-funded project published in 2006).
study_b_sample_and_data: Short norm-science/human-rights commentary and empirical synthesis on children's right to water in India without a formal methods section or fieldwork dates. Quantitative empirical evidence consists of 55 handpumps across 18 villages in Madhya Pradesh, Bihar and Jharkhand (24 rejected by mothers for drinking and cooking; 3 relying on irrigation tubewells), 44 public handpumps in villages of Madhya Pradesh and Bihar (9 located in backward-section localities) and field observations of arsenic removal plants and tapped surface water in West Bengal and fluoride removal plants in Madhya Pradesh, supplemented by brief unquantified references to rural and urban pockets and upper-caste norms in MP, Bihar and Gujarat.
overlap_rationale: Both full texts are readable and share lead author Nandita Singh. Study B (a 6-page Dialogue piece in Development co-authored with Lund University sociology-of-law colleagues) re-frames the core ethnographic rural India fieldwork reported in Study A (a 20-page empirical article in Gender, Technology and Development) from women and bureaucratic water technology governance to children's right to water under a norm-triad framework. The empirical passages in Study B reproduce the exact same underlying fieldwork data and near-verbatim prose and endnotes as Study A: (1) 55 government-installed handpumps in Madhya Pradesh, Bihar and Jharkhand, of which 24 were rejected for drinking and cooking due to colour, odour, taste and freshness, with reliance on wells and only 3 cases using distant irrigation tubewells (reported as 17 villages in Study A vs 18 villages in Study B); (2) qualitative observations of arsenic removal plants and tapped treated surface water in West Bengal and fluoride removal plants in Madhya Pradesh being rejected for drinking and cooking due to taste, smell and cooking suitability; (3) only 9 public handpumps in Madhya Pradesh and Bihar actually sited within Scheduled Caste, Scheduled Tribe or backward-caste localities (out of 46 handpumps in Study A vs 44 public handpumps in Study B), paired with the same Planning Commission (1980) 99-village benchmark citation; and (4) near-identical endnotes defining caste hierarchy (Béteille 1996) and dominant caste control (Srinivas 1959). Study A additionally reports sub-analyses from the same fieldwork on 15 women trained as TRYSEM handpump mechanics and 12 village panchayats (PRIs), whereas Study B lacks a standalone methods section and adds only brief unquantified mentions of girls' school dropout rates, urban pockets and Gujarat (Note 7). Treating both papers as independent empirical studies would directly double-count the identical handpump rejection and caste-exclusion sample.

study_a_sample_and_data: Ethnographic fieldwork conducted between 2002 and 2004 across 27 rural villages in India: 12 villages in two districts of Madhya Pradesh (Datia and Shivpuri, including villages Lamkana and Saprar) and 15 villages in three districts of West Bengal (including village Raipara). Data collection comprised participant observation (including Panchayat/committee meetings), structured and unstructured key-informant interviews, an earlier opinion survey in 12 village Panchayats, and 12 focus group discussions (5 exclusively with women), with roughly two-thirds of participants involved in local water governance bodies (PRI Women and Child Welfare and Health Committees in MP and NGO-initiated arsenic removal plant water quality management committees in WB).
study_b_sample_and_data: Interdisciplinary actor-oriented and sociology-of-law analysis drawing on multi-site field observations in India (collection dates not stated), reporting empirical subsets including: (1) 18 villages with 55 handpumps installed under rural water supply programmes in Madhya Pradesh, Bihar, and Jharkhand (24 rejected by mothers for drinking/cooking); (2) 44 public handpumps in villages of Madhya Pradesh and Bihar (only 9 located in backward-section localities); and (3) qualitative field observations of arsenic removal plants and treated surface-water taps in West Bengal, fluoride removal plants in Madhya Pradesh, and unspecified rural and urban pockets, examining barriers to children's and girl children's right to safe water.
overlap_rationale: Both full texts are accessible and authored or led by Nandita Singh, drawing on multi-site ethnographic fieldwork on rural drinking water supply and community water treatment in India. Study A (Singh 2006) analyzes 2002-2004 fieldwork in 12 villages across two districts of Madhya Pradesh (Datia and Shivpuri) and 15 villages across three districts of West Bengal, focusing on adult women's participation in Panchayati Raj Institution water committees (WCWHCs) and NGO-initiated arsenic removal plant committees, including case studies of public handpumps sited in dominant-caste localities in MP and purity/pollution barriers in WB. Study B (Singh et al. 2008) examines children's (especially girl children's) realization of the human right to water using broader multi-site Indian fieldwork (dates unspecified) that includes 18 villages with 55 handpumps in Madhya Pradesh, Bihar, and Jharkhand, 44 public handpumps in Madhya Pradesh and Bihar (only 9 sited in backward-caste localities), fluoride removal plants in MP, arsenic removal plants in West Bengal, and rural/urban pockets. Thus, the two papers are neither duplicates nor exact same-sample companion reports, as Study B includes additional states (Bihar, Jharkhand, and a note on Gujarat), fluoride plants, and handpump-level counts focused on children, whereas Study A focuses on governance committees in 12 MP and 15 WB villages. However, both draw on Singh's overlapping rural fieldwork on public handpump caste-locality siting in Madhya Pradesh and community arsenic removal plants in West Bengal, creating partial sample overlap and moderate double-counting risk if caste-based exclusion from rural handpumps or arsenic plants is synthesized across both studies without adjustment. Confidence is medium because Study B omits exact fieldwork dates and district/village names, preventing exact quantification of the village-level intersection in MP and WB.
